q: Do ruminant-derived Campylobacter jejuni vs C. coli MLST clonal complexes (CC-21/42/206 for jejuni; CC-828 with ST-827/2097 dominance for coli) show reproducible host-preference divergence from human clinical isolates across European ruminant cohorts, and does this divergence reflect true ecological host adaptation versus sampling bias?
basis: This replication confirmed 16/16 exact MLST matches with the paper's ST-827/2097-dominant coli (all in CC-828) and ST-21-dominant jejuni (CC-21/42/206) structure in Ocejo 2021's northern-Spain ruminant collection, but only tested 16 of 70 isolates and did not re-run the paper's full-cohort population-structure/phylogeny analysis (C10 not reproduced). The paper reports a clean two-species genomic separation (jejuni GC 30.4-30.5%, coli 31.2-31.5%, independently confirmed here to +/-0.1% GC in all 16 isolates), but whether the CC-828/CC-21 host-preference signal generalizes across other European ruminant surveys or is confounded by geography/farming-system remains untested.
next_steps: Reanalyze all 70 Ocejo isolates plus published European ruminant Campylobacter WGS cohorts (Ireland, France, Netherlands, UK) using an identical 7-gene MLST + core-genome MLST pipeline; compare CC frequency distributions between ruminant and human clinical PubMLST entries with permutation testing; stratify by farming system (beef vs dairy vs sheep vs goat) to separate host-signal from herd-management confounders.

q: What is the population-level convergent-resistance-mutation frequency for the tet(O) / aphA-3 / gyrA-T86I trio across European ruminant Campylobacter, and does convergence reflect independent selection under farm-level antimicrobial pressure or clonal spread of a few dominant resistant lineages?
basis: This replication independently reproduced gyrA Thr86Ile in all 13 CIP/NAL-resistant isolates (with the paper's documented WT exception C0268), tet(O) presence in 8/9 TET-R assemblies (three additional TET-R C. coli confirmed tet(O)-positive at raw-read level: 148/155/161 hits vs 0 in the susceptible control C0444), and mosaic tet(O/32/O) in C. jejuni C0437 - matching the paper's mechanism list. The 16-isolate subset shows every mechanism operates as claimed, but frequency estimates and phylogenetic distribution of convergent acquisition events require the full 70 isolates plus comparator cohorts, which was outside subset scope.
next_steps: Assemble a European-ruminant Campylobacter WGS meta-cohort (>=500 isolates from >=5 countries), compute per-gene phylogenies (tet(O), aphA-3, gyrA) mapped onto core-genome trees, and use ancestral-state reconstruction to distinguish independent horizontal-acquisition events from clonal descent; correlate with country-level antimicrobial-use data (ESVAC) to test whether convergent frequencies track selection pressure.

q: What is the true ruminant-to-human Campylobacter foodborne-transmission risk from raw-milk and undercooked-beef exposures relative to the well-established poultry-source dominance, and does the CC-828 C. coli signal in ruminants translate to appreciable human clinical burden?
basis: Ocejo 2021 characterized 70 ruminant isolates from beef cattle, dairy cattle, and sheep in northern Spain and this replication confirmed the CC-828 dominance in C. coli (11/9 coli isolates in the 16-subset carried ST-825/827/2097/1055/1595, all in CC-828) - but the paper is a genomic-characterization study, not a source-attribution study. It reports the ruminant reservoir composition without directly quantifying transmission to human cases. The extent to which these ruminant CCs appear in European human clinical Campylobacter surveillance (versus the poultry-dominant CC-21/45/48 jejuni signal) is not addressed by the paper or this replication.
next_steps: Perform a source-attribution study using the Ocejo ruminant isolates plus PubMLST/EnteroBase human clinical Campylobacter data from Spain and neighboring countries, applying Bayesian source-attribution models (STRUCTURE, iSource, or Hald-type genomic attribution); stratify human cases by reported exposure (raw milk, undercooked beef, poultry) to test whether ruminant-CC signals appear preferentially in ruminant-exposure cases.

q: Does the gyrA Thr86Ile fluoroquinolone-resistance mutation carry a measurable fitness cost in Campylobacter, and does resistance revert following cessation of enrofloxacin use on ruminant farms?
basis: This replication independently reproduced gyrA Thr86Ile in 13/13 CIP/NAL-resistant isolates (with WT Thr86 in all 3 CIP-S isolates including C0025, C0430, and the paper's documented CIP-R exception C0268). The paper documents high FQ-resistance frequency in the ruminant collection consistent with historical enrofloxacin veterinary use, but is a cross-sectional genomic snapshot: it does not track resistance frequency over time before/after antimicrobial-use policy changes, nor does it measure fitness costs in vitro or in colonization models.
next_steps: Design a longitudinal sampling study across Spanish ruminant farms with documented enrofloxacin-cessation dates (post-2018 EU veterinary AMR restrictions), collecting Campylobacter isolates at baseline and yearly intervals for gyrA-T86I frequency tracking; complement with in vitro growth-competition assays between isogenic gyrA-WT and gyrA-T86I strains in ruminant caecal-content culture, and chicken/calf colonization competition experiments.

q: Are the genomic adaptations and MLST clonal-complex host-signatures observed in cattle Campylobacter reproducible across sheep and goat isolates, and do cross-ruminant-species comparisons reveal distinct or shared adaptive signals?
basis: Ocejo 2021's 70-isolate cohort spans beef cattle, dairy cattle, and sheep (northern Spain); this replication's 16-isolate subset was chosen for mechanism-representativeness (every AMR gene, the ST-827 blaOXA-489 pocket, the C0268 exception) rather than for balanced species-of-host sampling, and the paper's per-host-species subgroup analyses were not re-run in this replication (C10 out of scope). Whether the CC-828 coli dominance and CC-21 jejuni dominance patterns hold uniformly across beef, dairy, sheep, and goat, or whether host-species-specific ST-signatures exist, is not settled by the tested subset.
next_steps: Stratify the full 70-isolate Ocejo cohort by host species (beef/dairy/sheep, and integrate goat isolates from other published European studies) and compute per-host-species MLST-frequency distributions with chi-square/Fisher testing; run per-host-species core-genome GWAS (e.g. Scoary, pyseer) against curated accessory-gene tables to identify host-species-specific accessory-genome signatures independent of AMR.
